whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state and its cities, towns, and counties can't charge a tax or fee based on how many miles you drive, and can't track or limit your driving miles unless you agree to it. It wouldn't cover government vehicles, or commercial trucks that cross state lines under an interstate fuel-tax agreement.

parts.label: No tax or fee based on miles driven
parts.what: The state, and any county, city, town or other local government, could not charge a tax or fee based on the number of miles a person drives.

parts.label: No tracking your miles without your consent
parts.what: Those same governments could not monitor or limit how many miles a person drives unless that person voluntarily agrees to it.

parts.label: Two exceptions
parts.what: It would not cover commercial vehicles that operate in more than one state where an interstate agreement exists for reporting fuel taxes or registration fees, and it would not cover vehicles owned and operated by the state or a local government.

whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so state and local governments — including public schools, universities, and community colleges — can't favor or disadvantage anyone based on race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public jobs, education, or contracting. It would also bar them from making people state support for race-based diversity, equity, and inclusion ideas to get a job, admission, or a scholarship; bar spending public money on offices at public schools whose role is promoting race-based preferential treatment; and bar discipline policies that treat students or employees differently by race or ethnicity. The proposition lists specific exceptions.

parts.label: No preferences and no discrimination by race, sex or national origin
parts.what: The state, cities, towns, counties, public universities, community colleges, school districts and other local governments could not give preferential treatment to, or discriminate against, people or groups based on race, sex, color, ethnicity or national origin in public employment, education or contracting — even where it is part of a federal program.

parts.label: No required statements of support
parts.what: They could not require applicants, employees, students or contractors to endorse or support race-based preferential treatment as a condition of admission, graduation, hiring, promotion, certification, contracting or a scholarship. That includes asking someone for a written or spoken statement supporting the race-based diversity, equity and inclusion ideas the measure identifies, asking them to confess race-based privilege or discuss their own or others' race, preferring someone for opinions they expressed if those opinions are based on race or ethnicity, and requiring a training or course that promotes those ideas.

parts.label: No public money for offices that promote preferences
parts.what: They could not spend public money to run or contract for an office or position at a public school, college or university whose job is promoting preferential treatment or discrimination based on race or ethnicity — including spending to influence who is on the faculty or in the student body, or on trainings, programs, activities and policies designed with reference to race, ethnicity, intersectionality, gender identity or sexual orientation, except as the measure otherwise provides.

parts.label: No discipline policies that differ by race
parts.what: They could not use any disciplinary policy or practice that treats students or employees differently on the basis of race or ethnicity.

whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so school districts can't use public money, staff time, or district communication systems to support unions, and can't take union dues out of employees' paychecks. Each school district employee would negotiate their own pay, benefits, and working conditions — the state and school districts would be barred from negotiating with a union on employees' behalf. It would override existing agreements and take effect January 1, 2028.

parts.label: No public money or resources for union operations
parts.what: A school district could not use public money or public resources to support a labor organization's operations, and could not use them to carry out labor organization activities during working hours.

parts.label: No union dues taken out of a paycheck
parts.what: A school district could not deduct any payment for labor organization membership dues from an employee's paycheck.

parts.label: No district communication systems for union material
parts.what: A school district could not give access to its internal communications systems to distribute labor organization recruiting information or political materials, and district employees could not distribute written, printed or digital communications on a labor organization's behalf in a way that uses public resources.

parts.label: Each employee negotiates for themselves
parts.what: Every school district employee would have the right to negotiate their own pay, benefits and working conditions, and the state and its local governments could not negotiate an agreement with a labor organization about school district employees' terms and conditions of employment.

parts.label: Existing agreements would be overridden
parts.what: It would supersede any school district contract, memorandum of understanding, meet-and-confer agreement, policy, ordinance or other written or spoken agreement.

parts.label: Starts January 1, 2028
parts.what: The measure would apply beginning January 1, 2028.

whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution on elections: only U.S. citizens could register and vote; voters would show valid government-issued ID before casting a ballot in every election; voters would get the option to have their ballot counted at their voting place on election day; and foreign nationals couldn't spend money to influence Arizona elections. It would let the legislature and the voters pass election laws — including on early and mail voting — if the laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest, and would apply to elections from January 1, 2028.

parts.label: Only U.S. citizens may register and vote
parts.what: It would reaffirm that only United States citizens may register to vote and vote in Arizona elections, and that Arizona elections are decided solely by the votes of eligible citizen voters.

parts.label: Government-issued ID before casting a ballot
parts.what: Voters would have to present valid government-issued proof of identity before casting a ballot in every election, as prescribed by law.

parts.label: The option to have your ballot counted where you vote
parts.what: Voters would have to be given the option to have their ballot tabulated at their voting location on election day.

parts.label: No foreign money in Arizona elections
parts.what: Foreign nationals could not contribute or spend money or anything of value to influence an Arizona election, and no person could accept such a contribution.

parts.label: A standard future election laws would have to meet
parts.what: The people and the legislature could pass laws governing elections, including early voting and mail voting, if those laws are rationally connected to a legitimate state interest — the measure names timely and accurate results, efficient election administration, election security, and preserving public confidence in election integrity.

parts.label: The legislature would have to pay for it
parts.what: The legislature would be required to appropriate any money necessary to carry the measure out.

parts.label: Applies to elections from January 1, 2028
parts.what: It would apply to all elections taking place on or after January 1, 2028.

whatItDoes: Would change the Arizona Constitution so the state can't take money out of a state-run scholarship account belonging to the child of a military family — someone serving on active duty, or killed in the line of duty — where the account can pay tuition at universities, community colleges, or accredited private colleges. Any later law violating this rule would be entirely void. Closing an account for reasons like illegal activity, choosing to close it, graduating, or not enrolling for four years after high school wouldn't count as taking the money.

parts.label: The state could not take back the money
parts.what: The state could not seize, transfer or otherwise take money from the scholarship account of a child of a military family — a child of someone serving or who has served on active duty, or who was killed in the line of duty — where the program is run by the state, treats such children who meet enrollment requirements as eligible, and lets the money be used for tuition or fees at state universities, community colleges, or private accredited colleges.

parts.label: A later law that breaks this would be void
parts.what: If the legislature passes a bill, or voters pass a ballot measure, on or after November 1, 2026 that violates those protections, the entire bill or measure would be void.

parts.label: What would not count as taking the money
parts.what: Closing an account because of illegal activity, closing it voluntarily, not renewing it, graduating from a college, or not enrolling in one for at least four years after finishing high school would not count as taking the money.

whatItDoes: Would change Arizona's school-voucher (ESA) program. Starting in the 2027–2028 school year, families making over $150,000 a year couldn't join (children with disabilities, and children eligible before 2022, excepted). Unspent account money would be transferred out each year, mostly to a classroom fund. Schools, tutoring businesses, and individual tutors would have to register with the state, pay annual fees, and fingerprint staff who are alone with students before being paid with ESA money — and ESA money couldn't buy items designated noneducational or luxury goods. The Attorney General would enforce the rules, and the committee that sponsored the proposition could sue participating families and schools over violations.

parts.label: A $150,000 family income limit
parts.what: From the 2027-2028 school year, children who would otherwise qualify but whose annual family income is over $150,000 — adjusted each year, or a lower figure set by the legislature — could not enrol in the empowerment scholarship account program. The limit would apply no matter how many children are in a family, and would not apply to children who would have been eligible before 2022, including children with disabilities.

parts.label: An unrenewed account closes after one year
parts.what: An account would stay open for one school year rather than three if the parent does not renew the contract.

parts.label: Leftover account money moves to the classroom site fund
parts.what: Each July 1 the Arizona Department of Education would take whatever money is left in a student's account and transfer 90 percent of it to the classroom site fund — every two years rather than yearly for a student with a disability — with a portion going to the Department or the State Board of Education to carry out and enforce the measure.

parts.label: The sponsoring committee could sue families and schools
parts.what: The political action committee that sponsored the measure would have the power to sue the families and private schools taking part in the program over any violations of it.

parts.label: Permanent disqualification for intentional misspending
parts.what: A parent, student or account holder found to have intentionally misspent account money would be permanently barred from the program, the account would be closed, and any money left in it returned to the state.

parts.label: Quarterly public reports and Attorney General enforcement
parts.what: The Department of Education would file quarterly reports with the attorney general and post each one on its website. The attorney general would enforce the rules for the money, and anything recovered as restitution would go into the classroom site fund.

parts.label: Removes a court protection for participating schools
parts.what: It would repeal today's requirement that, when a state law about the program is challenged in court, the state must prove the challenged law is necessary and does not put an undue burden on qualified schools.

parts.label: New limits on what the money can be spent on
parts.what: Tuition and fees could only go to schools that register with the Department and meet requirements including fingerprinting staff who have unsupervised contact with students and disclosing testing. Tutoring and teaching could only be bought from a registered qualified tutor, or through a school, business or accredited facility at a registered location. The supplemental materials that can be bought would change; items designated non-educational or luxury goods could not be bought at all; and unless the student has a disability, the money could not be paid to a member of the student's family.

parts.label: Annual registration for schools, providers and tutors
parts.what: From July 1, 2027, schools, tutoring providers and individual tutors would register each campus or location with the Department every year, pay an annual registration fee, and show they meet safety, location, non-discrimination, accreditation and fingerprint requirements. They would be subject to the same laws on investigating and disciplining misconduct that apply to public school employees. Families could not be reimbursed for payments to anyone unregistered, and registration forms and supporting documents would be public records.

parts.label: $1,750,000 moved from the medical marijuana fund
parts.what: On the day the measure takes effect, $1,750,000 would move from the medical marijuana fund — which has paid for clinical research, the Arizona teachers academy, public health initiatives, substance abuse prevention and administrative costs — to the Department of Education, the State Board of Education, the Department of Public Safety and the attorney general, for the administrative spending the measure requires.

parts.label: The rest survives if part is struck down
parts.what: If any part of the measure is found invalid, the rest would be unaffected, and the invalid parts would be interpreted as far as the law allows.

whatItDoes: Would limit city and town taxes on groceries — food and sealed nonalcoholic drinks meant for home use. New grocery taxes and any rate increases would need voter approval and couldn't go above two percent; a city already at two percent or more couldn't raise its rate at all; and no new grocery tax or increase could happen between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

parts.label: Existing food taxes capped, and some frozen outright
parts.what: A city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that approved a tax or fee on food and certain ready-to-drink non-alcoholic beverages in closed containers for home consumption on or before January 1, 2025 could only raise the rate with voter approval, and never above two percent of the tax base. If the rate on that date was already two percent or more, it could not be raised at all.

parts.label: A new food tax would need a vote
parts.what: A city, town or other taxing jurisdiction that had not approved such a tax or fee on or before January 1, 2025 would need voter approval to adopt one and to raise it afterwards, and it could not be more than two percent of the tax base.

parts.label: A freeze from June 30, 2025 to June 30, 2027
parts.what: No new tax or fee could be adopted and no rate could be increased between June 30, 2025 and June 30, 2027.

whatItDoes: Would declare that drug cartels — groups engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit, or terrorism — are terrorist organizations, and would require the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means within its authority to address threats they pose. It states that it does not support an asylum claim under federal law.

parts.label: Declares drug cartels terrorist organizations
parts.what: It would declare that drug cartels — associations of people engaged in human smuggling, drug trafficking for profit, or any act of terrorism — are terrorist organizations.

parts.label: The state homeland security department would have to act
parts.what: It would require the Arizona Department of Homeland Security to use all lawful means available within its authority to address the threats drug cartels pose.

parts.label: Not a basis for an asylum claim
parts.what: It would declare that the measure does not support a person's claim for asylum under federal law.

whatItDoes: Would require school and college sports teams in Arizona to be designated male, female, coeducational, or mixed, and would prohibit athletes whose original birth certificate records them as male from playing on female teams. Restrooms, locker rooms, and shower rooms tied to athletics could only be used according to the sex recorded on the athlete's original birth certificate. It would also expand who can sue over alleged violations.

parts.label: Female sports limited by sex recorded at birth
parts.what: Males could not play in female interscholastic and intramural sports, decided by the biological sex of the athletes as recorded at birth on their original birth certificates.

parts.label: Every team would have to be labeled
parts.what: Public and private schools and athletic associations that sponsor an interscholastic or intramural team or sport would have to expressly designate it as “males”, “men”, “boys”, “females”, “women”, “girls”, “coeducational” or “mixed”.

parts.label: Locker rooms and restrooms by sex recorded at birth
parts.what: Public schools, private schools, higher education institutions and athletic associations that provide private spaces integral to athletics — restrooms, locker rooms and shower rooms — could not authorise anyone to use a space not designated for their biological sex as recorded at birth on their original birth certificate.

parts.label: More people could sue and be sued
parts.what: It would expand who may sue and be sued over alleged violations of the law.

parts.label: Matching and coed teams unaffected
parts.what: It would not restrict any athlete's eligibility to play on a team or in a sport that matches their sex, or one designated coeducational or mixed. “Athlete” would cover students and any individual who takes part in a team or sport.

whatItDoes: Would ban speed and red-light cameras (photo enforcement) unless a local government already has a camera contract in place before December 31, 2026. A local government with an existing contract would have to ask its voters at the next general election whether to keep the cameras: a no vote shuts them down within 90 days; a yes vote keeps them for 10 years, with a fresh vote every 10 years after that.

parts.label: No photo enforcement without an existing contract
parts.what: A local authority or state agency could not use a photo enforcement system for speeding or traffic control device violations unless it had a contract in place before December 31, 2026 to operate one.

parts.label: Existing systems would go to the voters
parts.what: A local authority with a contract in place before that date would have to ask voters at the next general election whether it may keep operating the system. If voters say no, it would have to stop within 90 days of the election.

parts.label: Ten years, then another vote
parts.what: If voters approve, the system could keep running for ten years. At the end of each ten-year period the local authority would have to go back to the voters for another ten.

whatItDoes: Would require large Arizona school districts — 7,500 or more students, or any district with a school in a county of 500,000 or more people — to spend at least 60 percent of their operating money on direct classroom instruction, with the state auditor general defining the terms. Districts below that line would have to raise the share each year, and districts that don't comply would lose part, and eventually all, of their classroom site fund allocation unless granted a waiver.

parts.label: At least 60 percent spent on classroom instruction
parts.what: Every school district with at least 7,500 students, or that runs a school in a county of at least 500,000 people, would have to spend at least 60 percent of its operational spending on direct instructional expenses.

parts.label: The auditor general would write the definitions
parts.what: The auditor general would define what “direct instructional expenses” and “operational spending” mean for this requirement.

parts.label: Half a percent a year to catch up
parts.what: From the 2027-2028 fiscal year, a district spending less than 60 percent would have to raise the share it spends on direct instruction by at least half of one percent a year until it complies.

parts.label: Classroom site fund money withheld for non-compliance
parts.what: A district that does not comply would lose 25 percent of its classroom site fund allocation for each year it did not comply, up to the whole allocation after four or more years, unless a waiver is granted. The money not distributed would go to complying districts the following school year.

whatItDoes: Would let Pima County permanently raise the state-set limit on how much money it is allowed to spend — its “expenditure base” — by $70 million, with that amount adjusted every year afterward for population growth and inflation. The county says that if voters approve it, the spending limit for 2027–28 would rise by about $610 million, from about $817 million to about $1.43 billion. A YES vote lets the county raise its 1979–80 base limit; a NO vote does not. The Pima County Board of Supervisors put it on the ballot.

Would let the Vail Unified School District keep spending up to 12.5% more than the state's revenue control limit each year, for 2027/2028 and the next six years. The district says this continues about $5.1 million above the alternate budget for 2027/2028, at an estimated $1.61 per $100 of a property's secondary assessed value. A YES vote continues the override; a NO vote ends it.

Would let the Sahuarita Unified School District keep spending up to 15% more than its normal day-to-day “maintenance and operations” budget. Only voters who live in the district decide it, at the November 3, 2026 election. A YES vote continues that extra spending; a NO vote ends it.

Would let the Tanque Verde Unified School District keep spending up to 15% more than its normal day-to-day “maintenance and operations” budget. Only voters who live in the district decide it, at the November 3, 2026 election. A YES vote continues that extra spending; a NO vote ends it.
